couple things worth pushing on before you commit to the order:

  the slide-6 fight with Devon isn't really about position number. it's whether retention sets up growth as the payoff or whether it just drags. if retention lands as "here's why customers don't leave and the ones who survive the first 90 days actually expand," then growth on slide 6 isn't buried — it's earned. the test is: can a B person read retention and feel the question "ok, and how fast is that growing?" in their head before you get there. if yes, slide 6 is fine. if retention reads as a defensive story on its own, growth will feel late no matter where you put it.

  the cohort revenue + who-expanded-after-90 thing is the strongest retention move you have. way stronger than logo retention alone. that probably wants to be the lede of the retention section, not a supporting chart. "we lose some logos in the first quarter, the ones who make it past day 90 expand meaningfully, here's the cohort shape" is a story B people haven't seen a hundred times. plain NRR is a hundred times.

  on gross margin — if services is anywhere in that number, don't lead with the headline. lead with the carve. "75% blended, 82% on product-only contracts" or whatever the actual split is. B people will haircut a dev-tools GM number they haven't seen decomposed. if services isn't in there at all, say that explicitly on the slide — the absence of a footnote is itself a signal.

  the "market bigger than our current wedge" slide — is that a TAM slide or an expansion-argument slide? those are different slides wearing the same clothes. TAM/SAM/SOM is the version Devon's expecting. "here's why the wedge extends into X and Y" is a growth slide with a market costume on. pick one before you build it or Devon will think you're dodging the TAM question and you'll think you're making the expansion case.

  one thing i'd flag on the efficient-growth framing — net new ARR + expansion in the same frame is the right instinct, but make sure the decomposition is honest. if expansion is carrying the number, say so. B people can read a stacked bar. pretending it's balanced growth when it's really expansion-heavy will hurt you the second someone asks.

the actual defensible claim you're reaching for — sturdier, not just faster — that's a good spine. it just needs retention to land first or the rest sounds like a normal B deck with extra steps.

what's the cohort shape actually look like? if you've got the 90-day survival expansion data clean, that's probably the single most quotable slide in the whole deck.

  2. Two distinct Mercury bars worth separating:
- Functional: the chain works (oauth succeeds, sync fires, invites send, admin page renders).
- Self-serve: a customer walks it cold without Scaffold touching it — every error message has to be its own answer, every dead-end has to recover.

"Without us hand-holding" is the second one, and it's where the slack lives. The first is mostly already there; the second is where each link becomes its own product surface — and where the scope will keep accreting tabs (per your own framing).

Two questions that usually cut this kind of creep in half:
- For Mercury v1, do we need every source type self-serve, or is one reference connector (say, the Postgres one) enough to prove the path?
- Is admin self-serve "the page exists and works" or "the page exists, works, and a non-technical owner can recover from the bad states we'd historically have fixed for them"?

Those two answers usually shrink the scope back to shippable. Worth pinning before it eats another week of tabs.

CLERK
- What: hosted JS-first auth SaaS with pre-built UI components, session mgmt, and orgs/roles/invites out of the box
- Upsides: fastest path to a polished auth UX; RBAC + invites baked in; strong DX for Next.js/React
- Biggest worry: MAU-based pricing scales painfully; sessions/users live in their system so switching cost is real if priorities shift

AUTH0
- What: mature enterprise CIAM platform (Okta-owned), broad protocol support — SAML, SSO, SCIM, OIDC
- Upsides: battle-tested at scale; deep SSO/SCIM coverage buyers expect; solid compliance posture
- Biggest worry: fragmented pricing (rules/actions, MFA, B2C/B2B tiers); heavier integration than dev-first tools

CUSTOM AUTH
- What: build it yourself — sessions, hashing, OAuth/OIDC, MFA, reset — on Lucia, NextAuth, or your own code
- Upsides: full control over schema and flows; no per-MAU bill; nothing leaves your infra
- Biggest worry: you own every edge case — session rotation, reset abuse, MFA, SOC2 scope — and security bugs are yours

Short version: you're not being unreasonable, and your read on Auth0 is the right read. Self-serve pricing that stops at "talk to sales" before you hit a real number for core MAU is a known pattern with Auth0 — fine if you're past it, hostile if you're evaluating. The "fine, but not starting from" framing is exactly the right test.

A few honest points before the vendor list:

- Auth0's "free" tier is ~7,500 MAU and then steps fast; B2C and enterprise SSO land squarely on the "contact sales" side of the wall. That tracks with your experience, not just bad luck.
- "Pricing page says enough by not saying enough" is a fair heuristic for any infra pick that touches every user. If a vendor won't publish the curve for the tier you'd realistically need 12 months from now, treat that as the curve.
- The "weird enterprise add-ons later" worry is real — passwordless, adaptive MFA, org/team pricing, and B2B SSO are the usual hooks where a "good self-serve" provider quietly becomes "call us." Worth checking explicitly on whatever you land on.

Alternatives worth a real look, in roughly the order I'd consider them for a B-round startup that wants published pricing and a sensible core-auth bill:

- **Clerk** — strongest self-serve story right now. Public per-MAU pricing, free up to ~10k MAU, paid plans published. B2B/SSO is on a higher tier but the prices are on the page. Best if you want the modern DX and the bill stays predictable. Known weak spots: complex enterprise org features are newer than Auth0's, and SMS/voice MFA gets pricey if you lean on it.
- **WorkOS** — different shape. Free for self-serve consumer auth; their paid product is essentially B2B SSO/SCIM/Auth0-like Directory. If your real need is "let our enterprise customers log in with their IdP" rather than consumer MAU, this is the right tool. They publish pricing.
- **Supabase Auth** (if Postgres is already your data plane) — generous free tier, published overage pricing, OSS core. Cheapest honest answer if you're not on a vendor lock-in path.
- **Keycloak / Ory / Logto** if "no black box" is the *primary* criterion. Self-hosted or fully open pricing models. Real cost is your team's time, not a vendor line item. Worth it only if you actually have the bandwidth to own it; not a default choice at your stage.
- **AWS Cognito** — under-owned by people who don't realize how good it is for cheap MAU, but the DX is rough and B2B SSO ergonomics are worse than the others. Mention it for completeness; I'd pass.

The honest move is probably Clerk for core auth now, with a clean abstraction so a WorkOS-shaped B2B add-on can be slotted in later without re-platforming users. That's the path that survives "weird enterprise add-ons" without you starting from a black box.

Want me to draft a short Loom-style 3-bullet on this for the team channel, or a one-page eval doc comparing Clerk vs WorkOS vs Auth0 on price/SSO/migration cost? Either is cheap; tell me which is more useful.

Five things worth verifying before pulling the Clerk trigger — these are the "cursed limitation" candidates:

1. Org schema fit. Clerk's Organizations is their model (memberships, roles, invites baked in). If our shape needs anything exotic — nested orgs, a user in multiple orgs with different roles per app, B2C + B2B on one account — that's the wall. Worth a 30-min spike with a real org tree before commit.

2. SSO pricing tier. Enterprise SSO/SAML isn't on the base Clerk plan; it's the higher tier. If SSO is "later but real" for our motion, model the cost at 100 / 500 / 1k seats — that's the line item that bites mid-sales-cycle, not on day one.

3. MAU curve. Base pricing is fine; the jump is at the growth tier. Run the math against our 12-month projection plus a 3x upside case so we're not negotiating the bill mid-push.

4. JWT claims + org webhooks. Can session tokens carry org_id, role, and our internal user_id? Are the member-added / member-removed / role-changed webhooks complete enough for our audit story? That pair defines how much app-side glue we end up writing.

5. Offramp. Real-world export of users + orgs + memberships if we rip Clerk out in 18 months. That's the actual "undo in 9 months" reality check — not the marketing export.

If those five clear, Clerk is right given the eng-time math. The two things that'd flip me back to custom: org model doesn't fit the shape we need, or the SSO tier cost is a non-starter for our pipeline. Everything else is solvable with app-side code on top of Clerk.

Three moves, in this order. The order matters — if you point to the framework before you acknowledge the question, it reads as a deflection.

1. Acknowledge (one sentence). "Good question" / "fair to put on the table." Don't apologize, don't pivot. Jake's likely been sitting on this; naming that he asked is itself useful.

2. Frame the process (two or three sentences). The point is to make comp feel like a system, not a Morgan-decision. Something like: "Comp decisions here aren't something I make between 1:1s — they run on a cadence tied to [round close / Q1 review / annual cycle], and that's when I can give you a real answer."
   - True.
   - Gives you somewhere to point next time he asks, without re-debating.

3. Don't promise, but don't close the door (one sentence). "I can't commit to anything in this window, and I'd rather tell you that straight than hint at something I can't back up."

Things to actively avoid:
- "We'll figure it out after the round" — too specific, and Jake isn't on the investor loop, so don't let him start tracking round timing off your answer.
- "You're paid at market" — invites a market debate you don't want in a 1:1.
- "I'll fight for you" / "you deserve more" — creates a promise.
- "Let me check with Rishi / finance" — implies a process that may not exist and creates a follow-up expectation.
- Volunteering title / scope / role changes Jake didn't ask about. Answer the question he asked. Don't widen the negotiation in real time.
- Apologizing. Signals there's something to apologize for.

One judgment call: if Jake pushes ("when's the cadence", "what's the framework"), have a specific answer ready. "Q1 review tied to last full year" or whatever the actual cadence is — vague process answers sound evasive, which is the failure mode you're trying to avoid.

End state you want: Jake leaves feeling heard, knows the next checkpoint, and isn't expecting an off-cycle update. Anything beyond that is upside.

THE TRADE-OFF, SHARPENED

Honest usage-ramp logic captures the structural reality (broad directory, narrow live usage, ramp over months) but undersells in enterprise buying conversations where procurement needs a defensible budget number. A procurement floor that prices directory seats oversells the deployment we actually have on day 1. The decision isn't really "which model" — it's "what's the floor within a hybrid that matches the structural shape."

THE THREE MODELS

Pure MAU
  Captures: actual rollout, no overstatement, no awkward "we're paying for 110 seats but only 14 are live" conversation with security/procurement
  Breaks on: month-1 number (9-24 active devs across design partners) is too lightweight for procurement to defend internally; forecasting revenue off MAU is hard when the ramp window is 2-3 months
  Real risk: deal velocity stalls because contract size doesn't match the org's eventual footprint, even though the org hasn't earned that footprint yet

Pure seat / directory
  Captures: clean budget line, predictable PO, easy forecasting
  Breaks on: charges the org chart, not the rollout — Evergreen's 14 invited users vs. much-larger directory is the textbook example; customers will resent paying for access they haven't provisioned
  Real risk: misaligns price with value in the early phase, which is when the customer relationship is being set

Hybrid: platform floor + active-developer bands
  Captures: both sides — procurement gets a defensible minimum, price follows real ramp; structurally matches the pattern across all three design partners
  Breaks on: needs a clean counting rule for "active developer" (Devon's own caveat); risk of being quietly tied to directory seats, which would defeat the point
  Real risk: sales complexity if the rule isn't crisp; needs a one-sentence explanation that procurement and the customer's admin can both repeat back

WHY HYBRID IS THE ONLY STRUCTURAL FIT

Every design partner in Devon's data shows the same shape: directory materially larger than current active usage, narrow month-1, real ramp by month 3. Pure MAU prices the narrow month-1 and pretends the ramp isn't predictable. Pure seat prices the predictable ramp and pretends the month-1 narrowness isn't real. Hybrid follows the actual shape — broad access contracted, narrow usage billed, ramp tracked honestly. Devon's note ("bias toward floor + usage-ramp") already lands here; Tuesday's job is to set the floor without pretending every directory seat is live.

WHAT TUESDAY ACTUALLY NEEDS TO SETTLE

1. The floor itself
   - Fixed dollar figure (simple, defensible, but ignores customer size)
   - % of expected-ramp value (follows the contract but punishes slow rampers)
   - Minimum active-developer count (honest to usage, but weak budget signal)
   I'd push for fixed dollar tied to the smallest contract we'd be willing to deploy for, because procurement needs a number it can drop in a budget memo without explaining tiered math.

2. The counting rule
   - What counts as "active developer" — auth events, API calls, both, over what window
   - Has to be one sentence, explainable by both sales and the customer's admin
   - Do not tie it to directory seats or we're back to pure seat/directory in disguise

3. Band structure
   - Discrete tiers vs. continuous per-active-dev pricing vs. step-ups at threshold counts
   - Continuous is the cleanest for honesty; tiers are the cleanest for procurement. Pick one and own the tradeoff.

4. Evergreen specifically
   - 14 invited now, 45-60 with second admin group, 110-130 only if security/procurement expansion happens
   - If we price on the 45-60 range and the security expansion doesn't happen, we look overpriced. If we price on 14 and it does happen, we look underpriced.
   - Decide whether bands auto-ratchet (price follows usage) or are set at signing (price follows forecast).

5. Contract length and ramp protection
   - If month-1 is priced on 14 active devs, are we protected against a customer who never ramps? Annual commit with ramp-tracked bands is the obvious shape, but it locks in a slow customer at a floor that's too low.

OPEN QUESTIONS WORTH ANSWERING BEFORE TUESDAY

- What's the smallest contract we'd be willing to deploy for? That's effectively the floor.
- Do we have any signal on what procurement teams at these design partners actually need to defend internally — fixed dollar, % of spend, headcount-based?
- Is there a reference-customer story we can borrow — an industry-standard hybrid that procurement already accepts?
- For Evergreen specifically: is Sarah Kim's expansion timing knowable, or are we guessing?

I'd come into Tuesday ready to defend hybrid as the model and to argue hardest about the floor and the counting rule. Pure MAU and pure seat are reference points for what we'd be giving up, not real options.

THE QUESTION
Do we proceed with Northstar as the lead in roughly the shape Sofia has been describing, or do we reopen the process and try to create real price tension?

PATH A — Accept a workable Northstar-led round in roughly the shape described
- Oxygen: enough real breathing room to stop optimizing every decision for fundraising survival; tradeoff is that the headline is unlikely to be euphoric.
- Story: stays anchored to what we can defend now — Mercury activation/admin progress, bounded Evergreen signal, hybrid MAU pricing, expansion caveats intact.
- Diligence + legal: immediate refs, legal cleanup, January cash/runway work, governance work — all in parallel.
- Time cost: contained if Sofia is serious and the term sheet is workable.
- Hidden risk: we talk ourselves into "good enough" before we've pressure-tested the milestone language.

PATH B — Delay and widen the process
- Oxygen: only if widening actually produces a competing term sheet; otherwise weeks burned for no change.
- Story: defensibility erodes the longer we widen — more temptation to smooth over uneven expansion or tell a cleaner story than we have.
- Diligence + legal: same work as Path A, plus more repetition across firms and more founder cycles spent in process.
- Time cost: high — we burn operating time exactly while Mercury follow-through and enterprise gaps still need attention.
- Hidden risk: we turn it into theater and lose the ability to say we picked the narrow, defensible path on purpose.

THE TRADEOFFS WE KEEP UNDER-WEIGHTING

Price-shopping risk
- Upside on Path B exists only if we believe there is real price tension to create, not just theoretical upside.
- The market story does not get more defensible just because we spend extra weeks telling it to more people. Wider distribution of a softening story is not leverage.
- The cost of a failed widening isn't only the weeks — it's coming back to Northstar with less leverage and the same defendable story we had on day one.

Founder-cycle cost
- Path A founder cycles are bounded to one diligence cycle plus governance work.
- Path B founder cycles scale with the number of firms we engage, and pull focus from Mercury follow-through and the enterprise gaps that actually need attention.
- Founder cycles are also a quality cost on the defensible story — every retelling is a chance for the expansion caveats to drift.

2. Is the milestone language descriptive (how Northstar describes the bet) or wired into something we can't honestly control yet?

4. What is Northstar's posture on competition — willing to lead a competitive process, or sole-lead only?
5. Realistic close timeline, and what is the cash/runway implication if it slips a month?

WHAT WOULD CHANGE OUR MIND TOWARD PATH B
- A concrete signal that one or two additional firms would move in days, not weeks.
- A clear view that Northstar's milestone language is unworkable, not just unfamiliar.
- New information that materially weakens the Mercury / enterprise story.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE OUR MIND TOWARD PATH A
- Sofia confirms number, milestones, governance, and timeline in a shape that maps to what we can actually deliver in the next two quarters.

DECISION WE NEED TO MAKE ON THE CALL
- Path A contingent on (1), (2), (3), and (5) holding; otherwise reopen.

Bottom line: the draft is structurally sound for the core financing approval, but it has at least three real approval-mechanics gaps (stockholder consent is still a placeholder, the filing authorization floats free of stockholder approval, and the Sofia-seat / board-size language isn't anchored to the IRR/voting-agreement designation mechanic), and the cover paragraph plus two operative phrases read as if the round is on a signature track that it isn't on yet. Detailed list below — issue + safer wording, no rewrite.

A. Missing approval mechanics / structural gaps

1. Stockholder consent is still a "thought," not operative language. Section C is a placeholder summary note, and Section A only "recommends" stockholder approval. The packet needs a stockholder written consent draft (or a referenced form) alongside the board consent before counsel can clean mechanics. Ask Sarah to either draft Section C now or formally mark it as a blocker that travels with the packet.

2. No condition-precedent chain tying board consent → stockholder consent → charter filing. Section B authorizes filing the amended and restated certificate "at such time as the officer determines appropriate in connection with the closing" — but a DGCL § 242(b) charter amendment can't be filed before stockholder approval is in hand. Either add a closing CP ("the Company shall not file the amended and restated certificate until the stockholder consent... has been delivered") or move the filing authorization to a separate post-closing officer action.

3. Board-size / Sofia-seat resolution is freestanding. "The authorized size of the Board shall be increased by one director seat" works only if board size lives in the bylaws (or isn't fixed in the charter). Cross-reference: if board size is set in the charter, the bylaws can't override it and the resolution is inert; if it's set in the bylaws, this resolution is fine but the bylaws also need to be amended at or before closing. Either way, the operative language should say "the Board hereby increases the authorized size of the Board to [N] and directs the officers to amend Section [X] of the bylaws accordingly, effective at closing" — and it should reference the IRR/voting-agreement designation mechanism for the Northstar seat so the consent doesn't drift from the operative designation document.

4. Existing preferred class consent is unaddressed. If Scaffold has Series Seed/A preferred, the existing charter/voting agreement almost certainly requires a class vote of that preferred to create a new senior series. Section C lists a generic stockholder approval but not the separate class-consent path. Confirm whether the existing preferred has class approval rights and, if so, add a separate class-consent path to the packet.

5. Option-pool refresh is not in the packet. Most Series B rounds include an employee pool increase as a closing condition (typically baked into the cap table but also surfaced in the board consent). If the term sheet includes a post-money pool, the board consent needs a resolution authorizing the new pool size and the reservation of shares.

6. Placement / finder fee authorization is missing. Section A authorizes the financing for aggregate gross proceeds of $18M but doesn't authorize payment of any placement agent fee. If there's a placement agent, add a resolution authorizing fees on customary terms; if there isn't, that's fine but worth a one-line officer certificate to that effect for closing.

7. "Non-material changes" in both Section A and Section B lacks carve-outs. Standard practice is to exclude from officer discretion anything that would change: (i) per-share price, (ii) aggregate gross proceeds, (iii) lead investor identity, (iv) board-seat identity, (v) class-vote thresholds, (vi) option-pool percentage, or (vii) any closing condition. Add an explicit carve-out list.

8. Director count in Section D unconfirmed. Three signature blocks assume three directors. If Scaffold has more, the consent won't be unanimous when signed. Confirm director count and add a signature block per director. Also add a counterparts/e-signature clause ("This consent may be executed in counterparts, including by electronic signature, each of which shall constitute an original and all of which together shall constitute one instrument") — needed for DocuSign circulation.

9. DGCL § 144 / interested-director confirmation. If any current director is participating in the Series B (pro-rata), § 144 disclosure and disinterested approval apply. Confirm no director participation; if there is, the recital and operative language need to address it.

10. Section 280G confirmation. If any disqualified individual could receive a payment that vests or accelerates on a change-in-control event tied to the financing, a 280G stockholder vote may be needed. Almost certainly N/A for a clean primary issuance, but counsel should affirmatively confirm and the packet would benefit from a one-line recital to that effect.

11. Bridge / convertible note conversion. If there are outstanding SAFEs, convertibles, or bridge notes, the consent (or a related officer certificate) should acknowledge they convert at the Series B per their terms, so the post-closing cap table is unambiguous.

12. Recital lists documents presented but not the term sheet itself. The recital names the SPA, A&R certificate, IRR, voting agreement, and ROFR/co-sale, but not the term sheet or lead-investor commitment letter. Add a one-line reference to the term sheet / commitment letter as part of "principal business terms presented" so the operative "substantially consistent with those presented to the Board" has an unambiguous anchor.

B. Language that reads too far past current state (specific quotes → safer wording)

1. Cover paragraph — close date:
   Current: "move promptly into closing on or about February 22, 2024"
   Safer: "with a target of closing in late February 2024, subject to final documentation and receipt of required board and stockholder approvals"
   Why: "on or about February 22" reads as a commitment and a date counsel will be asked to defend.

2. Cover paragraph — sequencing:
   Current: "put the final documentation and signature process on a short path once this consent is approved"
   Safer: "set up final documentation and signature circulation once both this consent and the required stockholder approvals have been obtained"
   Why: as drafted, the paragraph implies signature launch follows board consent; in fact signature launch follows the stockholder consent (especially for the charter amendment).

3. Section B filing authorization:
   *** "is authorized to file the amended and restated certificate with the appropriate state filing office at such time as the officer determines appropriate in connection with the closing"
   Safer: "is authorized to file the amended and restated certificate with the appropriate state filing office promptly after the stockholder consent approving the certificate has been delivered and the other closing conditions have been satisfied"
   Why: closes the gap between board authorization and the § 242(b) prerequisite.

4. Section A officer-authority omnibus:
   Current: "Morgan Chen and Devon Hayes, acting singly, are authorized and directed to negotiate, finalize, execute, and deliver the transaction documents and to take any actions they determine necessary or advisable to effect the financing and the governance actions contemplated by these resolutions"
   Safer: same, but with a parenthetical "(excluding, for the avoidance of doubt, filing of the amended and restated certificate, which is governed by the resolution above)" — or carve out the charter filing to both officers acting jointly.
   Why: filing the charter is the most consequential single action in the financing; most companies require both officer signatures for charter filings even when they allow a single officer for everything else.

C. Cross-cutting housekeeping

1. Sarah's own flag — separate "director attention" from "officer / lawyer cleanup." Consider adding a Section E ("Administrative Actions Delegated to Officers") that lists the items in Section B explicitly as delegated, so directors reading the packet don't mistake housekeeping for substantive board items, and so counsel can mark them off without redrafting Section B.

2. Add a closing-date definition. Right now "closing" is used as a triggering condition in multiple resolutions but isn't defined. One-line definition in the recitals ("Closing" means the consummation of the Series B financing pursuant to the stock purchase agreement) eliminates ambiguity for the Sofia-seat and filing-effective resolutions.

3. Effective-date mechanics. Section D says "effective as of the date the last director signs below" — fine for a unanimous written consent. Just confirm Sarah's jurisdiction (Delaware § 141(f) by default, but Scaffold may be incorporated elsewhere) so the consent mechanic is the right one.

Things I deliberately did not do, per your instruction: no rewrite of the packet, no fabricated signature or stockholder consent text, no assumption that the financing is signed or approved. The list above is what I think should go back to Sarah before counsel sees it; the actual mechanics drafting (stockholder consent, class consent, counterparts, jurisdiction confirmation) belongs in her hands, not mine.

**Head of Customer Growth — revised draft**

**Reporting line:** reports to Morgan Chen. Partners with Devon Hayes on commercial strategy, with Sarah Kim on active customer threads, and with product / engineering on the gaps that recur across accounts (not on one-off asks).

**Why this role now**

Scaffold has moved past founder-led enterprise conversations and into the period where growth has to come from a repeatable motion, not from each deal being hand-carried by a founder.

Mercury is creating real pull from larger customers, and the question is no longer "can we land one?" but "can we build the motion that turns the next ten into a system?" We need someone who can answer that — by carrying forward what Mercury has already taught us, and by converting what Evergreen taught us about the cost of getting it wrong.

This leader will own the customer-growth motion end to end — acquisition, activation, conversion, expansion, retention — across the functions that today live inside founders' calendars. They will set up the conditions under which sales, CS, solutions, and demand-gen can exist as dedicated functions later, not run those functions in the meantime.

**What the role owns**

- The repeatable customer-growth / GTM motion around Mercury and the products that follow it — acquisition, activation, conversion, expansion, retention.
- The packaging and playbooks that make those stages work: positioning, pricing structure, security and procurement posture, onboarding, expansion triggers, renewal motion.
- Account strategy at the *pattern* level — which segments convert, where they stall, what expansion looks like — and feeding that signal back to product and engineering.
- A small set of senior customer relationships that anchor the motion, without becoming the person who carries them deal by deal.
- The operating cadence that makes the motion legible: forecasting grounded in patterns (not founder intuition), pipeline and conversion reviews, quarterly readouts on what's working and what's not.
- Working with Devon on pricing and commercial structure; with Sarah on the active customer threads that surface signal; with product and engineering on the gaps that show up across multiple accounts — not on the bespoke commitments that show up in one.
- Sequencing the team: defining when an AE, CSM, solutions, or demand-gen hire is the right next bet, and what each one unblocks.

**What this role is not**

- Not a VP of Enterprise Sales carrying a large team. There is no large team yet, and building the first wave of it is part of the job.
- Not a marquee-logo closer. The job is to make the next logo easier than the last one, not to trade bespoke product commitments for a reference.
- Not a "translate whatever the customer asks for into a roadmap" role. Bespoke asks get translated into patterns; patterns get fed to product. The motion does not bend per account.

**First 6 months**

- Ship the first version of the Mercury-era customer-growth playbook — positioning, activation, conversion, expansion, retention — and make sure it gets used, not just written.
- Convert what we learned from design partners and from Evergreen into motions we can run again, instead of lessons we keep re-learning.
- Establish a 6- and 12-month plan tied to the metrics that make the motion legible: funnel conversion by segment, activation rate, expansion triggers hit, retention by cohort — not just logos closed.
- Stand up the lightweight systems that let the team see the funnel without relying on a founder's memory: pipeline, forecast, conversion reporting.
- Identify the 2–3 product gaps that block repeatability most often, with concrete recommendations, and own the conversation with product on which to address in-quarter.
- Define the next 1–2 hires that would compound the motion, and what each one unblocks.

**Ideal background**

- 8+ years building customer growth at growth-stage SaaS, ideally Series A through C — comfortable owning the motion before the dedicated functions exist.
- Has built or significantly shaped a repeatable GTM motion around a product that has to win on substance, not on salesmanship.
- Has been through the founder-led-to-structured transition and knows what to build vs. what to defer.
- Comfortable working with product and engineering as a peer on positioning, packaging, and the gaps that block adoption across segments.
- Strong executive presence — can hold a CIO conversation when it matters — without making that the center of the job.
- Experience hiring and mentoring the first wave of customer-facing teams is a plus.

**Candidate signals we want**

- Has taken a technical, product-led motion from founder-led selling into a structured, repeatable growth engine — and can talk concretely about what they built, not just what they sold.
- Can name the failure modes: bespoke commitments that became permanent debt, packaging that didn't scale, sales systems that worked for one segment and broke for the next.
- Thinks in patterns and cohorts, not in logos. Comfortable saying "this account is an n=1; we shouldn't let it reshape the motion."
- Operates well in ambiguous environments where the product, the package, and the ICP are all still sharpening.
- Has been close enough to product to push back when a customer ask would create long-term drag.

**Draft positioning / candidate pitch**

- This is a hands-on builder role with direct influence on company strategy — not a late-stage carry-a-big-team VP slot.
- The right person will define how Scaffold wins and expands with larger customers over the next 12–24 months, and will be the reason the next account is easier than the last one.
- There is room to shape the motion, the packaging, the operating cadence, and the early team from the ground up.
- We have product pull (Mercury) and we have scars (Evergreen). The role is to convert both into a motion that compounds.

Revised screen below — drop-in for v1, same 30-min format and section structure. Three things the screen now actually tests, in this order: building motion from product-usage signal, product restraint, operating without a mature org underneath.

---

**Head of Customer Growth — recruiter screen plan v2**

**Recruiter screen length:** 30 minutes

**Recruiter goals**
- Confirm the candidate can extract repeatable adoption patterns from how customers actually use the product and translate that into a sales motion — not just inherit and run one.
- Confirm the candidate will refuse to over-promise product, and has a track record of walking away or restructuring deals rather than making commitments engineering can't keep.
- Confirm the candidate is comfortable being the senior commercial person on day one: closing deals themselves, building their own pipeline, partnering directly with engineering, before any team exists below them.

**Recommended flow**
- 3 min — company / role overview
- 5 min — candidate walk-through of what they personally *built* (not just ran)
- 10 min — product-driven adoption + product-restraint questions
- 7 min — operating-without-infrastructure questions
- 5 min — compensation, logistics, next steps

**Recruiter positioning notes**
- Position the role as the first senior commercial / growth builder around Mercury and the company's larger-customer motion.
- Be explicit that the first 6-12 months will be mostly individual contribution: prospecting, running technical conversations, writing the first expansion motion from product-usage signal.
- Emphasize founder-adjacency and cross-functional partnership over large-team management on day one.
- Candidate pitch should highlight room to shape the motion from observed customer behavior, the package, and the team over time.

**Core recruiter questions**

*Product-driven adoption (building the motion from how customers use it)*
- Walk me through a time you studied how existing customers were actually using a product — usage data, support tickets, expansion patterns — and turned that into a repeatable enterprise acquisition or expansion motion. What did you learn, and what did you change?
- Describe a motion you've built where the lead source was product-usage or customer-success signal rather than outbound. How did you operationalize it so it didn't depend on heroics?
- Tell me about a customer expansion that surprised you — either faster or slower than the product usage suggested. What did that teach you about the gap between usage and procurement?

*Product restraint (knowing when not to promise)*
- Give me an example of a deal where you had to walk away or restructure because the product wasn't there yet. What did you commit to, and what did you refuse to commit to?
- How do you typically pressure-test a product promise before it goes in front of a customer? Who do you loop in, and at what stage?
- Describe a time you had to tell an executive buyer "no, we can't do that yet" and still kept the relationship. What did you offer instead?
- When engineering has given you a roadmap date you don't trust, how have you handled selling against it?

*Operating without mature org*
- In your current or most recent role, what's the smallest team you've had around you, and what did you personally do that the team wasn't doing?
- Describe a sales motion you've built from a near-zero starting point — no SDRs, no marketing pipeline, no CS handoff. What did you do in weeks 1-4 that wouldn't show up on a dashboard?
- How do you stay close to product detail when you don't have a solutions engineer to lean on? Give a specific example of a technical conversation you ran yourself.
- What's the first system or process you'd build here in the first 90 days, and what would you explicitly NOT build?

**Desired signals**
- Has built a motion from product signal, not just executed an inherited one.
- Can name specific deals where they refused to over-promise and what they offered instead.
- Comfortable doing the work themselves in the first 90 days before delegating.
- Reads technical product detail closely and asks engineering-grade questions.
- Treats early customer behavior as a learning source, not just a pipeline source.
- Has operated as the most senior commercial person with no layer below them.

**Watch-outs**
- Spent career in large orgs with mature SDR / marketing / CSM layers.
- Pattern of "I hired great people and they executed" with no evidence of the system they built.
- Promises the roadmap to close the deal.
- Talks about enterprise adoption in brand-logo terms rather than usage-pattern terms.
- Wants the VP Sales title and a team before they'll do the work.
- Defers all technical detail to a SE.

**Scorecard**
- product-driven adoption instinct: 1-4
- product restraint and engineering partnership: 1-4
- operating without mature org / individual-contribution comfort: 1-4
- enterprise buyer credibility: 1-4
- compensation / logistics fit: 1-4

**If recruiter recommends pass, suggested hiring-manager topics**
- Reading product-usage data and turning it into pipeline / expansion
- A deal they personally closed where they had to refuse a product promise
- What they'd do in weeks 1-4 with no team
- How they'd partner with engineering on what's sellable vs. what's coming
- Founder handoff and account-ownership model

**Re: Pinecone connector verification docs wording**

Thanks — happy to clarify each of these against the current API v2 quickstart.

1. **Cursor stability across retries.** Page cursors returned by GraphQL API v2 are stable for at least the lifetime of the originating query. If a retry is needed due to a transient auth failure on a *specific page*, retry that page with the same `after` cursor — no need to restart from the prior successful page, and no need to drop already-fetched records. Only fall back to re-paginating from the previous cursor if the server explicitly indicates the cursor is invalid (e.g. an expired-paging error), which is distinct from a transient auth failure on an otherwise-valid request.

2. **JWT expiry during a retry.** Refresh the credential and replay the same GraphQL operation with the new bearer token. API v2 treats the request as idempotent within the standard retry window for operations that do not mutate state, so refreshing-and-replaying is the supported pattern. We don't recommend treating the operation as failed by default — that would force the connector to restart pagination unnecessarily. For mutation operations, follow the operation-specific idempotency guidance in the quickstart rather than blanket-replaying.

3. **In-place workspace token rotation.** Workspace-scoped tokens issued under the current connector auth model can be rotated in place — the connector calls the token rotation endpoint with the existing workspace-scoped token and receives a new one without requiring a customer-side reconnect. What this does *not* include: a self-serve admin endpoint, SSO-driven rotation, or any change to the header-only verification surface — those remain out of scope for this path. If Pinecone needs broader admin/SSO behavior, that's a separate conversation we'd want to scope explicitly rather than fold into the connector verification work.

Stale-packet reuse risks to check before regen (these are the failure modes I'd want ruled out, since HR can't see them from the PDF alone):
- **Export date stamp / footer** — a Mar 21 PDF export will often carry a "generated 2024-03-21" or version footer even if the table page is swapped. If that footer survives a partial regen, the candidate sees an older-dated packet. Worth a full-page PDF export, not a partial table swap, so the footer re-stamps to today.
- **Header / cover page** — same risk: "Confidential — Mar 21 draft" or a doc-id with the old date baked in. Cover page usually lives separately from the comp table.
- **Equity grant detail block** — 0.115% vs 0.125% usually pulls a share count (e.g. "X,XXX shares of common stock"). Share count is computed from % × shares outstanding as of grant date, so the old block will show the wrong absolute share number even after the % is fixed. Confirm the share-count line is also on Apr 2.
- **Vesting schedule / cliff language** — when sign-on and base move together, vesting start date and "cliff date" sometimes lag. If the Apr 2 packet moved start to "April/May 2024," the vesting commencement should match.
- **Sign-on repayment / clawback clause** — a new $10k sign-on usually carries a repay-if-leave-within-12-months clause. If the Mar 21 template had the $0 path with no clawback language, that paragraph may be missing.
- **At-will / employment classification boilerplate** — usually fine, but if Mar 21 vs Apr 2 changed any policy text (e.g. remote-work addendum, IP-assignment rider), it's somewhere besides the comp table.
- **Exhibit / equity plan reference** — "Subject to approval by the Board" date or the referenced equity plan name. Easy to miss.
- **Candidate name, address, start-date blanks** — not stale in the same way, but a partial regen that re-runs merge fields can reintroduce old placeholder text or strip a manually-filled field. Worth checking after.

The split you're describing is a classic internal-vs-external terminology trap. "Evergreen made the internal meaning clearer" usually means the internal taxonomy is fine and the friction is now entirely on what customers see in the UI, pricing page, sales calls, and docs.

2. "Overloaded" usually means one of three things — the same word is used for different things in different surfaces (settings vs billing vs invites), the word carries permissions baggage customers don't actually have, or the word doesn't match the verb customers use ("I want to add a teammate" vs "I want to invite an Owner").

Three add-ons for the Pinecone API v2 quickstart (retry/JWT section). Each stays inside the current GraphQL/JWT connector path — no token-rotation flow, no new connector semantics.

1) Paginated GraphQL retry after expired JWT

    cursor = FIRST_PAGE
    loop:
      try:
        page = graphql(cursor, jwt)
        process(page.items)
        cursor = page.next_cursor
        if cursor is None: break
      except 401:
        jwt = refresh_jwt()
        # replay SAME page with SAME cursor — do not restart
        # from the prior successful page
        continue

   Locks in: on 401 mid-pagination, refresh the JWT and replay the current page with the same cursor. Pagination does NOT restart from the prior successful page.

2) Mutation auth failure before resolver execution

    try:
      graphql(createOrder, jwt)
    except 401:
      # auth failed before resolver execution — no side effect
      jwt = refresh_jwt()
      graphql(createOrder, jwt)    # safe to retry

   Locks in: a mutation that 401s before its resolver runs has no side effect, so the same mutation can be retried once a fresh JWT is in hand. (401 after resolver execution is out of scope here.)

3) Unsupported token-rotation headers

   "Token-rotation headers are outside the current GraphQL/JWT connector path; the connector ignores them."

   Locks in: no inference of support from ignored headers, no rotation flow implied.

TITLE
API v2 — retry quickstart: JWT refresh + same-cursor GraphQL replay

USE WHEN
A v2 GraphQL request returns 401 / "token expired" mid-pagination, or a mutation needs auth-fails-before-resolver semantics confirmed.

RULES (v2-correct)

1. Same-cursor replay on 401. When a paginated connection query (`first` + `after`) returns UNAUTHENTICATED, refresh the JWT out-of-band and replay the request with the SAME `after` cursor and the SAME variables. Do not restart from `null`. Do not advance. v1 retry loops that restarted from page 1 are wrong for v2 — inserts between pages shift offset cursors and replay-from-start will skip or duplicate. Position is preserved only if the cursor is reused verbatim.

2. Mutations: zero side effect if auth fails before resolver execution. Auth is evaluated at the operation root, before any child resolver runs. An expired or invalid JWT produces a top-level UNAUTHENTICATED error and no mutation work happens — no DB write, no job enqueue, no event publish, no outbound webhook. Clients MUST NOT optimistically apply local state assuming partial success. v1 permitted some partial-execution-then-throw behavior; v2 does not.

3. No in-band token-rotation header flow. v2 does not support rotating the access token via a request header (e.g. `X-Rotate-Token`, `X-New-Access-Token`, `Authorization-Refresh`). Refresh is out-of-band: call the token endpoint, swap the bearer token in the client, then retry the original request. Any snippet that documents an in-request rotation header is stale v1 and must not ship.

REPLAY PATTERN

    cursor = null
    while True:
        result = graphql(query, { first: 50, after: cursor })
        if result.is_401_or_unauthenticated:
            refresh_jwt()          # out-of-band, no rotation header
            continue               # SAME cursor, SAME variables — do not advance
        yield result.page
        if not result.page.hasNextPage: break
        cursor = result.page.endCursor

    # Mutation variant: on UNAUTHENTICATED, refresh_jwt(), then re-send the
    # mutation with the SAME input. No local optimistic apply.

WHAT MAKES THIS SNIPPET STALE-AGAIN MARKERS (reject if you see these)
- "restart pagination from page 1 on 401"
- "rotate access token via header"
- "mutation may partially commit on auth failure"
- any reference to `X-Rotate-Token` / `Authorization-Refresh` / similar in-band rotation

OUT OF SCOPE (intentionally not covered here)
- Backoff/jitter on 5xx — separate retry guide
- Refresh-token rotation policy — handled by auth service, not client
- Webhook delivery retries — separate webhook doc

   (a) Product copy today: The UI label is "View activity history." It links to a present-state view of admin actions inside the workspace. There is no CSV, no downloadable report, and no file artifact behind that label.

   (b) Support explanation: If a customer asks what they can do with the page, support says it shows recent admin actions visible to the workspace admin, and that any reporting beyond that view goes through the customer's own logging pipeline (their SIEM, their exports), not through a built-in Scaffold export.

   (b) Support explanation: If a customer asks whether SSO is on or off, support points to the workspace admin's configuration page and confirms the state for that workspace, not bank-wide.

---

RUNBOOK EXAMPLE — Workspace / org-invite issue: stale migration label vs wrong target

When to use
- Customer reports an invite or membership landed in the wrong workspace, or shows a label they don't recognize.
- Suspected cause is old migration naming, not a real target mismatch.

Step 1 — Confirm the intended workspace (customer-visible)
- Ask the customer only for the workspace name they expected to land in.
- Use the current display name in all replies. Do not ask about prior names, old org labels, or migration history.

Step 2 — Internal lineage check (not customer-facing)
- Compare three things internally:
  - invite target workspace
  - membership record workspace
  - current workspace
- If all three resolve to the same workspace lineage, the check passes.
- If alias/rename history exists, treat it as a cross-check only — do not paste it into the reply, Zendesk note, or customer email.

Step 3 — Customer-safe wording
- Pass case: "We've verified the invite and membership record are tied to the intended workspace."
- End the message there. Do not mention the old label, prior org label, or replay.
- Do not paste raw workspace ids, archived labels, or migration text into any customer-touching surface.

Step 4 — When to stop and escalate
- Stop if checkpoint evidence is missing, partial, or inconsistent (no accept-event trace, no verifier output, or state doesn't match what the customer sees).
- Do not request manual replay from the customer thread.
- Do not tell the customer replay will be run.
- Collect before escalating: current workspace name + internal id, membership record target, invite target, source event id if any, verifier/accept-event trace if present, current customer-visible state, and whether alias history is just a rename vs a true target mismatch.
- Escalate to Atlas owner (Rishi) for review. Support keeps thread ownership until handoff.

Do not say to the customer
- "The archived label was X."
- "We'll run a manual replay."
- "The system lost your data" or any framing that implies missing state without owner approval.

Lane reminder
- Weekly support owner: thread + immediate next step.
- Leo: first-pass verifier/auth boundary read if needed.
- Jake: only if it becomes a sequencing or cut decision — not for migration-history debugging.

One-line summary for the runbook index
- Verify current workspace by lineage, not by quoting the old label; if checkpoint evidence is incomplete, stop and escalate to Atlas owner without promising replay.

Engineering, product, design, support, and everyone carrying customer context helped turn one-off setup work into something we can ship repeatedly. Atlas got stronger in the places that matter most once customers are live — better auth and verification, more usable webhook and connector behavior, clearer docs, faster first technical reads, and less thrash on issues that used to bounce around.

More important than any of those numbers, people kept showing up for each other while we were changing the product under real customer pressure. That takes judgment, patience, and a lot of follow-through that rarely gets enough credit.

Thank you for sticking with the hard parts, for caring about the details customers actually feel, and for helping build a company that learns and gets better instead of just getting louder.

We're proud of what this team shipped this year, and we're excited for what we can build from here.

Decision frame — pick by observed pain × frequency × workaround-availability, not by narrative.

The three legs, in order of weight:
1. Pain severity. Dead end (user stuck, no recovery) beats confusion (user wonders, finds their way) at equal frequency. OAuth cancel sounds like a true dead end; empty source-list is mostly confusion; invite-link status is usually confusion with a manual workaround. Treat that as the starting ranking unless Priya's final data says otherwise.
2. Frequency. Use confirmed support counts, not preliminary. Per-issue ticket volume across the same window, with categories split cleanly so one user hitting two issues doesn't get double-counted.
3. Workaround. If support can unstick the user in under a few minutes today, that issue drops a tier. If it escalates or eats a session, it climbs.

Adjust only by engineering cost. If two tie on the three legs, take the cheaper build. Don't let cost be the first tiebreaker — only the last.

What Priya should confirm before the call:
- Final ticket counts per category with the window and how the three buckets are defined.
- For each: does it block activation (user never reaches a working state) or just delay it (reaches it, with help)? Different problem class.
- Repeat rate — same user hitting it twice, or multiple tickets on one account.
- Workaround today — what support actually does, how long it takes, and whether any of these became escalations or long tickets.
- First-session vs. returning-user split, so we know if the fix is one-time onboarding gain or chronic.

What NOT to count as a roadmap reason:
- Speculative funnel lift or projected conversion impact without data behind it.
- Single-customer complaints treated as a priority signal without volume.
- Growth-narrative framing ("unlocks the activation story") — that's the language we're keeping out of this call.
- Granular admin-role logic as either a reason to ship or a reason to skip. It's scope, not signal.
- Strategic-priority labels ("table stakes," "best practice") with no observed pain tied to them.
- Hunches about what users probably want, including mine or yours.

Tiebreaker order if Priya's data lands roughly equal: dead end > confusion, high frequency > low, no workaround > workaround, cheaper build > pricier build. In that sequence, not all at once.

============================================================
Webhook Signing (Atlas)

Overview
Atlas signs every webhook delivery with an HMAC-SHA256 signature computed over a canonical request representation. Your server verifies the signature using a shared secret to confirm that the event came from Atlas and was not modified in transit. Every delivery is signed, including retries.

Delivery is best-effort. Atlas retries failed deliveries with exponential backoff for up to 24 hours, but individual delivery is not guaranteed. Endpoints should be idempotent and treat any webhook as potentially delayed or duplicated.

Headers on every delivery
Each webhook request includes:

  - `Atlas-Signature` — hex-encoded HMAC-SHA256 of the signature base string
  - `Atlas-Timestamp` — Unix epoch seconds at which Atlas created the event
  - `Atlas-Event-Id` — unique identifier for this specific event (use for idempotency)
  - `Atlas-Webhook-Id` — stable identifier for the webhook configuration

Treat the event id as opaque and use it to deduplicate.

Signature base string
The signature is computed over a single string:

    {timestamp}.{raw_request_body}

Where:

  - `{timestamp}` is the exact value of the `Atlas-Timestamp` header (Unix epoch seconds, integer, no fractional component).
  - `{raw_request_body}` is the exact bytes of the JSON body — do not parse, re-serialize, or reformat before computing.

The HMAC-SHA256 is computed with your webhook secret as the key, and the result is hex-encoded into the `Atlas-Signature` header.

Common mistakes that cause verification to fail:

  - Re-serializing the JSON before hashing ("pretty-printing," key reordering, whitespace normalization) produces different bytes and a different signature. Use the raw body.
  - Concatenating in a different order, or with extra delimiters. The format above is exact.
  - Hashing parsed fields rather than the body. Future Atlas versions may add fields; hashing the raw body keeps verification stable.

Timestamp handling and clock skew
`Atlas-Timestamp` is one of the inputs to the signature, so a modified timestamp invalidates the signature. Verification must use the timestamp from the same header the signature was computed over.

Atlas allows a small clock-skew window when verifying. This window exists to tolerate clock drift between your servers and Atlas; it is not a replay window and is not a substitute for replay protection on your side.

Recommended practice:

  - Reject events whose timestamp is more than 5 minutes in the past (configurable per webhook; default is 300 seconds).
  - Reject events whose timestamp is more than a small forward-skew window in the future (default is 60 seconds).
  - Maintain a short-lived cache of recently-seen event ids and reject duplicates.

Replay protection is the responsibility of the receiving system. The clock-skew tolerance absorbs drift; it does not protect against a deliberate replay.

Rotating webhook secrets
Atlas supports two active secrets per webhook endpoint (`primary` and `secondary`). Atlas signs deliveries with the `primary` secret; `secondary` is used only during rotation.

To rotate without downtime:

  1. In the Atlas dashboard, generate a new secret for the endpoint. Atlas writes it as the new `secondary`; the existing secret remains `primary`.
  2. Update your verifier to accept signatures from either secret. Both are valid during this overlap.
  3. Confirm your verifier is accepting the `secondary` secret by inspecting a recent delivery.
  4. Promote `secondary` to `primary`. The old `primary` is removed; future deliveries signed with it will fail verification.

Complete all four steps within 24 hours. If you skip step 4, your endpoint will start failing verification once the old `primary` is removed on the next rotation.

If you suspect a secret has been compromised, rotate immediately. Removed secrets cannot be recovered.

Test-mode events
Events delivered to a test-mode webhook are signed with the endpoint's `test` secret, not the live secret. The signing algorithm is identical to live events; only the secret differs.

Caveats:

  - Test events are not subject to the same replay-protection guarantees as live events. Use them for development and integration testing only.
  - Do not verify test events against a live secret, or live events against a test secret. Mixing secrets produces signature failures that resemble clock-skew or rotation problems.
  - Test events are delivered only to endpoints explicitly configured as test-mode. Live endpoints never receive test events.

Verification steps
A complete verification routine:

  1. Read the raw request body before parsing JSON.
  2. Read `Atlas-Timestamp` as an integer.
  3. Read `Atlas-Signature` as a hex string.
  4. Compute HMAC-SHA256 of `{timestamp}.{raw_body}` with your webhook secret. Compare to the header in constant time.
  5. Confirm the timestamp is within your accepted tolerance window (defaults: 300s past, 60s future).
  6. Check `Atlas-Event-Id` against your dedupe cache; reject duplicates.
  7. Only then parse the body and process the event.

If any step fails, return a non-2xx response. Atlas retries per its standard backoff schedule.

If verification still fails
If you have followed the steps above and verification still fails, support can investigate. Please provide:

  - The `Atlas-Event-Id` and `Atlas-Webhook-Id` from the failing delivery.
  - The exact `Atlas-Timestamp` value at the time of receipt.
  - The endpoint URL (or webhook id) and which secret was active.
  - The raw request body and the signature value your verifier computed.
  - The output of the diagnostic snippet below, run against your environment.

    import hmac, hashlib, sys
    ts = sys.argv[1]
    body = open(sys.argv[2], "rb").read()
    secret = sys.argv[3].encode()
    mac = hmac.new(secret, f"{ts}.".encode() + body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    print(mac)

If the diagnostic output does not match the `Atlas-Signature` header, the most common causes are body re-serialization or the wrong secret. If it does match and Atlas-side verification still disagrees, escalate with the inputs above.
============================================================

---

Verifying JWTs from the Scaffold API

When a request is rejected because a token can't be verified, the cause is almost always one of a few things on the caller side. The checks below cover what we've seen in practice; the token format and signing requirements themselves haven't changed.

  - Clock skew. Token validation compares iat, nbf, and exp against the API server's clock. If your server's clock is more than a minute or two off, a valid token can look not-yet-valid or already expired. Confirm your host's time sync (NTP, chrony, etc.) before anything else.
  - iat / nbf / exp values. Make sure iat is a past timestamp, nbf is not in the future, and exp is still in the future. A common mistake is using a Unix timestamp in milliseconds where seconds are expected, or vice versa — that puts all three fields well outside the expected window and verification fails immediately.
  - Stale keys after a key rotation. If you cache the signing key (or a JWKS endpoint response) locally, a rotation can leave you verifying new tokens against an old key. Refresh your key material on the same schedule as the issuer rather than relying on a long-lived cache.
  - Signing secret or algorithm mismatch. The token must be signed with the secret or key you configured for the environment you're calling, and with an algorithm the API accepts for that environment. Mixing a staging secret against prod (or the other way around) is the most common version of this and produces a verification failure that looks like a bad signature.

If you've worked through these and a token still won't verify, file a support ticket with the token's iss, iat, exp, and the request id from the failed call, and we'll take a look.

---

    When a JWT-authenticated request to Atlas fails authentication, work through these checks in order. First, clock skew between your service and the token issuer — even a few seconds of drift will cause tokens to fail validation against their `iat`, `nbf`, or `exp` claims. Second, verify those time-based claims are present and well-formed; a missing or malformed timestamp is treated as invalid. Third, if you rotate signing keys, confirm the validating client has refreshed its key set — a cached old key will reject newly-signed tokens until it updates. Finally, check that the signing secret or public key configured in Atlas matches what your issuer is currently signing with; a mismatch rejects otherwise well-formed tokens. These are the standard checks for any JWT integration.

USE THE RAMP. Hesitation at the steps is a pain signal, not stubbornness; forcing stairs is the fastest way to turn "mild arthritis" into a flare. Ramp it both directions.

SHORT AND FLAT: ~10-15 min, flat sidewalk only, no hills, no curbs if avoidable. Cut the usual loop in half. Goal is bathroom + sniff time, not cardio.

WHY THIS LOOKS THE WAY IT DOES: barometric pressure drops on damp days aggravate arthritic joints — this is the pattern the "no rain walks" rule was built around, and the fact that he walked normally on flat means the joints themselves are fine, the steps are the problem.

NOT A VET CALL TODAY: he ate, he's bright, he walked off the hesitation on flat ground. That's the "manage at home" profile.

VET-CALL TRIGGERS (any one, same day):
- Sudden regression — won't or can't use the ramp he used yesterday
- Limp that doesn't resolve after a few minutes of walking, or comes back worse after rest
- Pain signs: whining, panting, or flinching when you touch or lift him
- Won't get up from rest, or bunny-hopping on the back legs
- Won't eat, vomits, or can't settle (restless, pacing)
- Visible joint swelling, heat, or a new limp on one specific leg

Decision rule (one sentence, then the conditions):

Tapering proceeds when the standard alert split alone would lead to the same action as the extra logs would. Re-engage automatically the moment they would diverge.

"Same action" holds when, for at least one business cycle (call it 48h):
- the split cleanly separates endpoint-local (support/info) from queue-wide events
- queue-wide delay stays in normal range
- no dropped events

Re-engagement triggers (no one should have to argue to turn them back on):
- any queue-wide anomaly
- any dropped event
- a new endpoint pattern the alerts don't classify
- any recurrence of the original incident class

If any of those fire, logs come back on and stay on until the same three conditions hold again. Symmetric — we don't keep them off by inertia any more than we kept them on by inertia.

Most intermittent "not-before" failures trace back to one of three things: (1) copying a sample/timestamp from docs or a tutorial, (2) a host clock that's drifted (containers, VMs, and laptops coming back from sleep are common culprits), or (3) rounding/precision when the value is generated in seconds instead of a numeric date.
- A sample timestamp from our docs is the most likely cause here — those are illustrative, not long-lived, and they drift out of the tolerance window quickly. Please generate `nbf` fresh from your server's clock at token-creation time (epoch seconds, integer), and set `nbf` to the current time (not a few minutes "in the future" to give yourself headroom).

Things to check on your side:

- `nbf` is the integer seconds-since-epoch at the moment you mint the token, not a copied value.
- The host minting tokens has a synced clock (NTP / chrony; AWS / GCP / Azure instances are usually fine out of the box — bare metal and containers less so).
- Don't reuse tokens across processes with different clocks; mint per issuer.

If after checking those you're still seeing intermittent failures, please send:

- The exact `nbf` value you're sending (decoded payload is fine),
- A rough timestamp of the failure from your logs,
- The host/region minting the token.

We treat those as fresh signal and will route to eng only if it looks like a code-path issue. Happy to dig in.

— Support

Subject: Re: [their subject]

Hi [name],

Thanks for the detailed report — wanted to share a quick frame on how signatures work and the checks that usually clear this up.

Atlas webhook signatures are HMACs computed over the exact bytes of the request body as it arrives at your endpoint. Any transformation between receipt and verification — even invisible ones like JSON key reordering, whitespace normalization, or Unicode escaping — changes the bytes and breaks the match. This most often comes from middleware that parses the body into an object and reserializes it before the verifier sees it.

A few concrete checks, in order:

1. Log the raw request body immediately on receipt (before any parsing) and feed that exact byte sequence to the verifier. If mismatches disappear here, a transformation is happening upstream of verification.
2. If your framework auto-parses JSON bodies (e.g. express.json() in Node, request.body vs request.data in Django, Flask before_request hooks), confirm the verifier is reading the raw stream, not the parsed object.
3. Verify against a payload replayed byte-identically from our event log / dashboard. If the signature matches there but not in your environment, the drift is local.
4. Temporarily bypass body-parsing middleware and re-run the replay. If the mismatch clears, you've found it.
5. Confirm your HTTP server/client isn't applying charset normalization or content-encoding rewraps before the verifier reads the body.

If you can share the language/runtime and a small redacted snippet showing how the body reaches the verifier, I'll take a closer look. Happy to jump on a quick call if that's easier — just let me know a time.

Best,
[signature]

Subject: Re: Atlas API v2 — intermittent 401s on token verification

Hi [name],

Thanks for the detailed report on the intermittent 401s in the [date/window] window. We pulled the verifier logs for the failing requests and want to share what we found before we dig further.

What we observed
- The JWTs attached to the 401 responses had `iat` and `nbf` claims roughly six minutes ahead of our verifier's clock at the moment of the request.
- Per RFC 7519 (§4.1.5 / §4.1.6), our verifier rejects tokens whose `nbf` is materially in the future — that's intended behavior, not a regression. We do apply a small leeway window for normal clock drift between hosts; six minutes sits outside that window.
- During the same window, your side reported an NTP issue tied to a deploy. That's consistent with the drift we see in the claims — i.e., the tokens were minted against an issuer clock that had drifted forward, and our verifier correctly treated them as not-yet-valid.

Putting it together, the failure pattern matches clock skew on the issuer side rather than an authentication defect on ours, and we don't believe a code change on Atlas is needed to resolve it.

If you still believe we rejected a token whose `iat`/`nbf` was inside the documented leeway, please send us:
  1. The full JWT strings (header.payload.signature) from the failing requests.
  2. The request IDs and approximate UTC timestamps from your side.
  3. `chronyc tracking` (or equivalent) output from the issuer host covering the window.
  4. NTP daemon logs from the same window.

With those we can replay the verification against our recorded verifier clock and confirm one way or the other. Happy to jump on a call if it's faster.

— Leo
Scaffold Support

Two problems, both bounded-claims issues:

- "Exactly once" is not a true statement for webhook delivery. Retries on transient failure (timeout, 5xx, connection reset) are how every webhook system handles unreliable endpoints — the draft even admits this in the next sentence. Calling it exactly-once and then describing conditions where duplicates occur is self-contradictory and will get quoted back at you by a customer who saw a duplicate.

- The carve-out ("unless your endpoint times out") undercuts the whole claim. Timeout is the dominant retry trigger, so in practice every receiver needs dedup — meaning the "no duplicate handling" guidance is wrong for the majority of integrations. Also, timeouts aren't the only cause: 5xx from the receiver, network blips mid-handshake, and sender-side retries after a deploy all produce duplicates with no timeout on the receiver's side.

- (Aside) The framing "send us logs, we'll investigate whether a replay defect occurred" implies duplicates are a sender bug. Sometimes they are, sometimes they're expected retry behavior — receiver-side idempotency handles both correctly, and the support contract should say so.

Recommended shape (at-least-once + receiver-side idempotency, which matches your prior guidance in memory for 504s): "Webhook delivery is at-least-once. If your endpoint returns a non-2xx response or times out, we retry. You should deduplicate deliveries using the event ID we include in the payload header — this handles retries on timeout, 5xx, and transient network failures. If you see a duplicate that can't be explained by a retry trigger, send us the delivery ID and we'll investigate."

Subject: Re: API v2 — 429s during batch metadata sync

Hi [name],

Short answer: the 429s aren't an instability signal — they're the API telling you it hit the configured quota for that account. Worth a quick read on the headers below, and you should be fine on the next sync.

**What the headers mean**

- `X-RateLimit-Limit` — requests per window for this token/account
- `X-RateLimit-Remaining` — what's left in the current window
- `X-RateLimit-Reset` — Unix timestamp when the window rolls over
- `Retry-After` (on the 429 itself) — seconds the server wants you to wait before retrying

You saw the 429s because the sync crossed the remaining quota in that window. Reset time was in the headers, so nothing was lost — the server just bounced the over-quota calls.

**Backoff — practical version**

1. Honor `Retry-After` exactly on the 429 response.
2. Between batches, check `X-RateLimit-Remaining`. When it's under ~10% of `Limit`, pause until `X-RateLimit-Reset`.
3. If you're doing aggressive parallelism, dial concurrency down to roughly `Limit / window_seconds` requests/sec sustained, then add a small jitter (~10%) to avoid synchronized retries.
4. Retry on 429 with full-jitter exponential backoff (cap ~30s, ~5 attempts). Don't retry on 4xx other than 429.

**When to send us request IDs**

You don't need to for normal 429s — the headers above are enough. Loop us in with the `X-Request-Id` header values (and timestamp window) only if you see any of:

- Sustained 429s at low concurrency (under 2 RPS sustained)
- Mixed 429 + 5xx on the same request
- 429s after you've fully respected `Retry-After`
- Anything where a sync genuinely failed mid-batch (we'll want to confirm no partial-state)

Happy to look at logs on any of those. Otherwise you're set — no action needed on your side beyond the throttle pattern.

Best,
[Leo]

Subject: Re: JWT verification failures

Hi [name],

Thanks for the details. Based on what you've described, this looks like it traces to two configuration items on your side rather than a platform incident.

Two things to check:

1. Server clock skew. JWTs use short-lived exp claims and are sensitive to clock drift. From the timestamps in your logs, your server clock appears to be running roughly seven minutes ahead of ours, which can cause valid tokens to fail verification as "expired." Sync your server against a reliable NTP source (time.cloudflare.com or pool.ntp.org) and confirm drift stays under ~30 seconds.

2. JWKS cache after key rotation. Atlas rotates signing keys on a documented schedule. If your JWKS cache TTL is longer than the rotation interval, you'll keep verifying against a key that's already been retired. Drop your cache TTL to something under the rotation window (one hour is a safe default) and re-fetch on rotation.

If you've checked both and you're still seeing failures, reply with the request IDs (X-Request-Id headers from the failed calls, ideally 2–3 of them) and the corresponding timestamps and I'll dig into the logs directly.

Happy to clarify any of the above — let me know how it goes.

Best,
Leo
Atlas Support

---
**To:** [Acme integration lead]
**Subject:** Re: API v2 webhook — duplicate deliveries on metadata sync

Hi [name],

Thanks for flagging this. The duplicate deliveries you're seeing are the at-least-once delivery contract working as designed — not a bug on either side, and nothing's lost on our end. Quick rundown of what's happening and the small handler change that makes it go away.

**Why you're seeing duplicates**

When your endpoint times out (or returns a non-2xx), our delivery layer retries the same event with the same `scaffold-delivery-id` until it gets a successful response or the delivery window closes. Two timeouts during your sync test means two retries landed, and your handler processed both. That's the contract — we'd rather deliver twice than miss once.

**What your handler needs to do**

Make the handler idempotent on `scaffold-delivery-id`:

  - Read the header on every attempt (not just the first).
  - Record it before any side-effecting work.
  - On retry with a seen ID, return success without re-processing.
  - Only return 2xx *after* the event is durably committed — acking before commit is what causes unrecoverable duplicates.

**Quick things to verify**

  - Header is read on every attempt, not just the first.
  - Dedupe state survives handler restarts within the delivery window.
  - 2xx is sent after commit, not from middleware that acks early.

**If duplicates continue after this**

Send us the `X-Request-Id` from each duplicate delivery (one per duplicate is enough) and we'll trace them end-to-end on our side. That's the fastest path to a real diagnosis, and avoids us both digging through logs.

Happy to jump on a 15 if any of this is unclear — otherwise no further action needed from your side beyond the handler change.

Best,
Leo

---

Two drafts below, same core message: cursors are for active page sequences; checkpoint durably; resume from the last processed object on expiry; only escalate with request IDs if it persists after that.

----

CUSTOMER-FACING SUPPORT ANSWER (for Sarah to send)

Subject: Cursor pagination: resuming after cursor_expired_after_24h

Hi there,

Thanks for flagging this. cursor_expired_after_24h is the API telling you the cursor you supplied is older than 24 hours — it is expected behavior, not a data-loss signal or a defect.

What it means
  - A cursor identifies where the previous page ended. After 24 hours the API stops honoring it, so it returns the expiry error instead of a possibly-stale page.
  - Your pages that completed in under 24 hours are unaffected.

Recommended pattern
  - Keep using cursors while you are actively paging through a sequence.
  - Persist a durable checkpoint — typically the ID or timestamp of the last object you successfully processed.
  - If you hit cursor_expired_after_24h, resume from that checkpoint (e.g. starting_after the last processed ID, or created_after your checkpoint timestamp) rather than restarting the full sequence.
  - A full fresh poll every minute is not necessary and will hit rate limits; checkpointed resumption is the supported pattern.

If the expiry continues after you switch to checkpointed resumption, reply with the request IDs from the affected calls and we will trace the exact sequence. We do not expect to need them once the resumption pattern is in place.

Happy to review the code change with you if useful.

— Scaffold API Support

----

INTERNAL EXAMPLE WORDING (for Leo's cursor-pagination section)

Cursor pagination — handling expiry

Cursors returned by /v2/list are valid for 24 hours from issuance. They chain an active page sequence; they are not a long-term handle on your position.

Pattern
  - During an active page sequence, pass the cursor back unchanged.
  - Persist a durable checkpoint alongside each page: the ID (or created_at) of the last object you processed successfully.
  - If a sequence pauses longer than 24 hours and the cursor expires, resume from the checkpoint — query with starting_after set to the last processed ID, or created_after set to the checkpoint timestamp — rather than restarting the full sequence.
  - Escalate with request IDs only if the expiry persists after you are checkpointing and resuming this way.

Do not switch to a fresh full poll on expiry. Cursors with a checkpointed resumption are the supported pattern; fresh polling is unnecessary, scales poorly, and will hit rate limits.

Subject: Re: Nightly export worker — cursor + fresh polling

Hi [name],

Thanks for the detailed write-up. Quick summary of what I see: your worker completed a few cursor pages, crashed, and on resume you switched to `created_after` polling to avoid relying on a potentially stale cursor. That's a reasonable defensive choice — here's how it lines up with our contract.

Cursors are designed to traverse a stable result set within a run, not to be paused and resumed arbitrarily later. Once you stop, the underlying data can shift (new events being written, occasional backfills), so picking up an old cursor hours later isn't a supported resumption strategy. You can keep using cursors within a run; you just can't stitch an old cursor to a fresh `created_after` query without dedupe.

For your nightly export, the supported path is:

  - Treat the export as at-least-once. Expect overlap at the boundary between the cursor run and the fresh polling window.
  - Dedupe by event ID on your side. Make the downstream idempotent on event ID — that's the contract.
  - On resume, start fresh polling from the last successfully persisted event ID (or its `created_at`). Don't try to reuse the old cursor.

On the request IDs you shared — `req_cur_4418`, `req_cur_4419`, `req_cur_4420` — I had our team pull them. All three pages returned successfully on our side; there's no server error or data loss on our end to point at.

If you ever see behavior that doesn't match the documented contract — a cursor page that's inconsistent with the previous one, or a `created_after` query returning events in a shape you've already processed under a different ID — send the request IDs and we'll dig in.

Happy to jump on a 15 min call if it's faster than going back and forth here.

Best,
[Name]

Hi [name],

- What we saw on req_wh_9041 / 9042 / 9043: the first attempt hit a 502 from your endpoint, we retried per our published delivery contract, and the retry succeeded. Same event ID across attempts — no data loss, no extra payload.
- Why this happens: our delivery is at-least-once. On any 5xx (502 included) we can't tell whether the request landed before the error, so we retry. Exactly-once isn't something we promise — and on the open internet it isn't something anyone can honestly promise.
- What makes it exactly-once for you: dedupe on the `event_id` field in every payload (stable across retries). If you've already processed that ID, treat the next delivery as a no-op. A small in-memory or KV-backed set keyed on event ID, with a short TTL, is usually enough.
- When to send us request IDs again: if you see duplicates that aren't explained by a 5xx retry on your endpoint, missing events, or a payload mismatch (event ID changing between attempts), send the request IDs plus a timestamp window and we'll trace the delivery log end-to-end.

Happy to jump on a call if it's useful.

Best,
Sarah
